title: Fibre dimension bounds descend in affine inverse systems
statement: Let $I$ be a small nonempty directed partially ordered set. Let $(A_i)$ and $(C_i)$ be directed systems of commutative rings and let $A_i\to C_i$ be compatible ring homomorphisms, each of finite type [def-weil-pbc-finite-type-algebra]. For every $i\le j$ assume that the canonical map $A_j\otimes_{A_i}C_i\to C_j$ is surjective; the tensor product is the pushout of commutative algebras [lem-weil-pbc-algebra-tensor-pushout-universal-property]. Let $A=\varinjlim_iA_i$ and $C=\varinjlim_iC_i$, with the induced map $A\to C$ [def-weil-pbc-category-colimit]. Fix an integer $d\ge0$. For a prime $\mathfrak p$ of $A$ let $\kappa(\mathfrak p)$ be its residue field [def-weil-pbc-localization-at-prime]. Suppose that for every such $\mathfrak p$ the topological Krull dimension [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension] of $\operatorname{Spec}(C\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak p))$ [def-weil-affine-spectrum] is at most $d$. Then there is $i\in I$ such that, for every prime $\mathfrak p_i$ of $A_i$, the dimension of $\operatorname{Spec}(C_i\otimes_{A_i}\kappa(\mathfrak p_i))$ is at most $d$. Empty spectra have dimension $-\infty$ and are allowed.

source.place: Tag 05M5, label lemma-limit-dimension, affine specialization: surjectivity of the comparison ring maps gives closed immersion comparison morphisms.

proof.text: Put $X_i=\operatorname{Spec}C_i$, $S_i=\operatorname{Spec}A_i$ and let $f_i$ be induced by $A_i\to C_i$. Define $U_i$ to be the points whose local topological fibre dimension is at most $d$, and $Z_i=X_i\setminus U_i$. For each $x_i\in U_i$, this local dimension is a nonnegative integer $n\le d$ (the fibre point exists, so its neighbourhoods are nonempty). The ring-theoretic bounded-open-upstairs theorem, applied to $A_i\to C_i$ at $x_i$ with this $n$, gives an open neighbourhood all of whose points have local fibre dimension at most $n$, hence at most $d$. Thus $U_i$ is open as the union of these neighbourhoods, and $Z_i$ is closed. The affine fibre-product identification and the supremum-of-local-dimensions theorem say that $Z_i$ is empty exactly when every fibre of $f_i$ has dimension at most $d$. Assume for contradiction that every $Z_i$ is nonempty.

For $j\ge i$ and $x_j\in X_j$, write $x_i$ for its image and $s_j=f_j(x_j)$, $s_i=f_i(x_i)$. For a ring map $R\to T$ carrying a prime $\mathfrak q$ of $T$ back to $\mathfrak p$, the induced injection $R/\mathfrak p\to T/\mathfrak q$ extends to their fraction fields by $a/b\mapsto\bar a/\bar b$, since $b\notin\mathfrak p$ maps outside $\mathfrak q$; these are the residue fields. Thus $\kappa(s_i)\to\kappa(s_j)$ is the field map used below. The surjection $A_j\otimes_{A_i}C_i\to C_j$, after extending scalars to $\kappa(s_j)$, identifies $(X_j)_{s_j}$ with a closed subspace of $(X_i)_{s_i}\times_{\kappa(s_i)}\kappa(s_j)$. Surjectivity after tensoring is explicit: a pure tensor $c_j\otimes\lambda$ lifts by choosing a preimage of $c_j$, and sums lift termwise. The quotient-spectrum homeomorphism identifies this as a closed embedding. At corresponding points, local dimension in a closed subspace is at most that in the ambient space: choose an ambient open neighbourhood attaining its local dimension; intersect with the closed subspace, and every chain of irreducible closed subsets of the intersection is a chain of irreducible closed subsets of that neighbourhood. Taking the minimum over neighbourhoods gives the inequality. Field-extension invariance of local dimension applies to the finite type $\kappa(s_i)$-algebra $C_i\otimes_{A_i}\kappa(s_i)$ (the images of any finite set of algebra generators still generate). Consequently a point of $Z_j$ maps into $Z_i$.

Let $J_i$ be the radical ideal defining the reduced induced structure on $Z_i$, and put $D_i=C_i/J_i$. For $a\in J_i$ and every prime of $C_j$ belonging to $Z_j$, its contraction belongs to $Z_i$ by step 2, so the image of $a$ lies in that prime. The description of the reduced induced ideal as the intersection of these primes implies that $C_i\to C_j$ maps $J_i$ into $J_j$. Thus the $D_i$ form a directed ring system. Set $D=\varinjlim D_i$. The spectrum-colimit theorem identifies $\operatorname{Spec}D$ with the inverse limit of the nonempty affine schemes $\operatorname{Spec}D_i$, whose transitions are affine. Each is quasi-compact by quasi-compactness of spectra, so the nonempty-limit theorem supplies a point $z\in\operatorname{Spec}D$. The compatible maps $C_i\to D$ induce $C\to D$ and hence a point $x\in\operatorname{Spec}C$ with images $x_i\in Z_i$. No factorization from mere set containment of an arbitrary nonreduced scheme is used.

Let $s$ be the image of $x$ in $\operatorname{Spec}A$, let $k=\kappa(s)$, and let $s_i$ be its image in $S_i$. Fix $i_0\in I$ and restrict to $i\ge i_0$, a cofinal directed tail. To extend a compatible cocone from this tail to the whole system, for an arbitrary index $i$ choose $j\ge i,i_0$ and compose the transition from $i$ to $j$ with its cocone map; a common upper bound of two choices proves independence and compatibility. This gives the same colimit universal property on the tail. Put $B_i=C_i\otimes_{A_i}k$, using $A_i\to A\to k$. For $j\ge i$ the map $B_i\to B_j$ is surjective: extend the given comparison surjection along $A_j\to k$; the source identifies with $C_i\otimes_{A_i}k$ by $(a_j\otimes c_i)\otimes\lambda\mapsto c_i\otimes\bar a_j\lambda$, with inverse $c_i\otimes\lambda\mapsto(1\otimes c_i)\otimes\lambda$. The balancing relations make these ring maps well-defined, and their composites are the identity on pure tensors. Set $B=C\otimes_Ak$. This is the colimit of the $B_i$: compatible ring maps $B_i\to T$ amount, by the tensor pushout property, to compatible maps $C_i\to T$ and one map $k\to T$ (the restrictions to $k$ coincide by compatibility at common upper bounds) agreeing on every $A_i$. By the two colimit universal properties they amount precisely to maps $C\to T$, $k\to T$ agreeing on $A$, hence to a map $B\to T$. The point $x$ determines a point $\widetilde x\in\operatorname{Spec}B$, by the tensor pushout map $B\to\kappa(x)$ induced by $C\to\kappa(x)$ and $k\to\kappa(x)$. The field map $k\to\kappa(x)$ sends the fraction of classes $a/b$ to the fraction of their images; its denominator stays nonzero by contraction of the prime of $x$ to $s$, so the two maps agree on $A$.

The ring $B_{i_0}$ is a finite type $k$-algebra, since the images of the finite generators of $C_{i_0}$ over $A_{i_0}$ generate it over $k$. A field is Noetherian: its only ideals are zero and the whole field, generated by zero and one. The finite-type-algebra Noetherian theorem therefore makes $B_{i_0}$ Noetherian. For $i\ge i_0$ let $K_i=\ker(B_{i_0}\to B_i)$; these ideals are increasing and form a directed family. The maximal-ideal-in-a-set theorem supplies a maximal $K_{i_1}$ among them. For $j\ge i_1$ it follows that $K_j=K_{i_1}$; for any other $i$ a common upper bound shows $K_i\subseteq K_{i_1}$. All maps $B_{i_0}\to B_i$ are surjective. The kernel of $B_{i_0}\to B$ is exactly $\bigcup_iK_i$: an element maps to zero in the colimit exactly when it becomes zero at a stage, by the elementwise filtered-colimit theorem. That map is surjective as well: every colimit element has a representative in some $B_i$, and that representative lifts to $B_{i_0}$. Hence the canonical map $B_{i_1}\to B$ is an isomorphism, since both are the quotient of $B_{i_0}$ by $K_{i_1}$. Explicitly, to invert $B_{i_1}\to B$, lift an element of $B$ to $b\in B_{i_0}$ and send it to the image of $b$ in $B_{i_1}$. Two lifts differ by $K_{i_1}$, so this is well-defined; it preserves ring operations and is inverse on representatives.

The point $\widetilde x$ corresponds under $B_{i_1}\cong B$ to the point lying over $x_{i_1}$ in the field extension of the ordinary fibre of $f_{i_1}$ from $\kappa(s_{i_1})$ to $k$. Its contraction is exactly the fibre point of $x_{i_1}$, since both points are obtained by contraction of the maps to $\kappa(x)$. The fibre algebra $C_{i_1}\otimes_{A_{i_1}}\kappa(s_{i_1})$ is finite type over its field, so local-dimension field-extension invariance applies. Since $x_{i_1}\in Z_{i_1}$, the local dimension at $\widetilde x$ of $\operatorname{Spec}B$ is greater than $d$. But the hypothesis bounds the dimension of this entire fibre by $d$, and its local dimension is at most the entire dimension (the entire space is an allowed open neighbourhood). This is a contradiction.

Therefore some $Z_i$ is empty. At that stage every point of every fibre has local dimension at most $d$. Taking the supremum over the points of each fibre gives the asserted global bound. For an empty fibre this supremum is $-\infty$, so it imposes no exception.
